The `use cache` directive allows you to mark a route, React component, or a function as cacheable. It can be used at the top of a file to indicate that all exports in the file should be cached, or inline at the top of a function or component to cache the return value. Functions and components that use `use cache` must be async.

00001| --- 00002| title: use cache 00003| description: Learn how to use the "use cache" directive to cache data in your Next.js application. 00004| related: 00005| title: Related 00006| description: View related API references. 00007| links: 00008| - app/api-reference/directives/use-cache-private 00009| - app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents 00010| - app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheLife 00011| - app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheHandlers 00012| - app/api-reference/functions/cacheTag 00013| - app/api-reference/functions/cacheLife 00014| - app/api-reference/functions/revalidateTag 00015| --- 00016| 00017| The `use cache` directive allows you to mark a route, React component, or a function as cacheable. It can be used at the top of a file to indicate that all exports in the file should be cached, or inline at the top of a function or component to cache the return value. Functions and components that use `use cache` must be async. 00018| 00019| > **Good to know:** 00020| > 00021| > - To use cookies or headers, read them outside cached scopes and pass values as arguments. This is the preferred pattern. 00022| > - If the in-memory cache isn't sufficient for runtime data, [`'use cache: remote'`](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache-remote) allows platforms to provide a dedicated cache handler, though it requires a network roundtrip to check the cache and typically incurs platform fees. 00023| > - For compliance requirements or when you can't refactor to pass runtime data as arguments to a `use cache` scope, see [`'use cache: private'`](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache-private). 00024| 00025| ## Usage 00026| 00027| `use cache` is a Cache Components feature. To enable it, add the [`cacheComponents`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents) option to your `next.config.ts` file: 00028| 00029| ```ts filename="next.config.ts" switcher 00030| import type { NextConfig } from 'next' 00031| 00032| const nextConfig: NextConfig = { 00033| cacheComponents: true, 00034| } 00035| 00036| export default nextConfig 00037| ``` 00038| 00039| ```js filename="next.config.js" switcher 00040| /** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */ 00041| const nextConfig = { 00042| cacheComponents: true, 00043| } 00044| 00045| module.exports = nextConfig 00046| ``` 00047| 00048| Then, add `use cache` at the function, component, or file level. Cached functions and components must be async: 00049| 00050| ```tsx 00051| // Function level 00052| export async function getData() { 00053| 'use cache' 00054| const res = await fetch('https://api.example.com/data') 00055| const data = await res.json() 00056| return data 00057| } 00058| 00059| // Component level 00060| export async function MyComponent() { 00061| 'use cache' 00062| return <> 00063| } 00064| ``` 00065| 00066| When used at file level, every exported function becomes a cached function and must also be async: 00067| 00068| ```tsx 00069| // File level 00070| 'use cache' 00071| 00072| export default async function Page() { 00073| // ... 00074| } 00075| ``` 00076| 00077| ## How `use cache` works 00078| 00079| ### Cache keys 00080| 00081| A cache entry's key is generated using a serialized version of its inputs, which includes: 00082| 00083| 1. **Build ID** - Unique per build, changing this invalidates all cache entries. If [`deploymentId`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/deploymentId) is configured, it overrides the build ID for cache key purposes. 00084| 2. **Function ID** - A secure hash of the function's location and signature in the codebase 00085| 3. **Serializable arguments** - Props (for components) or function arguments 00086| 4. **HMR refresh hash** (development only) - Invalidates cache on hot module replacement 00087| 00088| When a cached function references variables from outer scopes, those variables are automatically captured and bound as arguments, making them part of the cache key. 00089| 00090| ```tsx filename="lib/data.ts" 00091| async function Component({ userId }: { userId: string }) { 00092| const getData = async (filter: string) => { 00093| 'use cache' 00094| // Cache key includes both userId (from closure) and filter (argument) 00095| const res = await fetch( 00096| `https://api.example.com/users/${userId}/data?filter=${filter}` 00097| ) 00098| return res.json() 00099| } 00100| 00101| return getData('active') 00102| } 00103| ``` 00104| 00105| In the snippet above, `userId` is captured from the outer scope and `filter` is passed as an argument, so both become part of the `getData` function's cache key. This means different user and filter combinations will have separate cache entries. 00106| 00107| > **Good to know:** When a cached function reads [root parameters](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/next-root-params), only the ones it actually reads become part of its cache key. 00108| 00109| ### Cache output 00110| 00111| A cached function produces the same output for the same inputs. The first call with a given set of inputs runs the function body and stores its output. Every later call with the same inputs reuses that output, within a render pass and across requests, for as long as the entry lasts. 00112| 00113| Outputs are stored by a [cache handler](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheHandlers), [in memory](#runtime-caching-considerations) by default, and last until they [revalidate](#revalidation). 00114| 00115| ```tsx filename="lib/orders.ts" 00116| import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache' 00117| 00118| export async function getOrderSummary(accountId: string) { 00119| 'use cache' 00120| cacheLife('hours') 00121| 00122| const orders = await getOrders(accountId) 00123| const totals = await getOrderTotals(accountId) 00124| 00125| return { orders, totals } 00126| } 00127| 00128| export async function getOrders(accountId: string) { 00129| 'use cache' 00130| cacheLife('hours') 00131| 00132| return db.orders.findMany({ where: { accountId } }) 00133| } 00134| 00135| export async function getOrderTotals(accountId: string) { 00136| return db.orders.aggregate({ where: { accountId }, _sum: { amount: true } }) 00137| } 00138| ``` 00139| 00140| In the example above, each `accountId` has its own entry for `getOrderSummary`, holding the serialized `{ orders, totals }` object it returns. Calls to `getOrders` have their own entries, keyed by the same `accountId`. If an earlier call, through the summary or directly, already filled one, `db.orders.findMany` doesn't run and those orders become part of the summary's output. See [nested caching behavior](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheLife#nested-caching-behavior) for how an inner lifetime affects the entry around it. 00141| 00142| Note that `getOrderTotals` is not cached. It is exported so other parts of the application can read fresh totals in an uncached scope. Inside `getOrderSummary`, though, the totals query only runs when that function runs following the `'hours'` lifetime set there. 00143| 00144| With [Cache Components](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents), prerendering fills the entry and keeps rendering, so this output contributes to the route's [static shell](/docs/app/getting-started/caching#prerendering) and can contribute to its [prefetch](/docs/app/getting-started/caching#prefetching). A cache life too short to store safely leaves a hole that resolves at request time instead. See [prerendering behavior](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheLife#prerendering-behavior) for the thresholds. 00145| 00146| ## Serialization 00147| 00148| Arguments to cached functions and their return values must be serializable. 00149| 00150| For a complete reference, see: 00151| 00152| - [Serializable arguments](https://react.dev/reference/rsc/use-server#serializable-parameters-and-return-values) - Uses **React Server Components** serialization 00153| - [Serializable return types](https://react.dev/reference/rsc/use-client#serializable-types) - Uses **React Client Components** serialization 00154| 00155| > **Good to know:** Arguments and return values use different serialization systems. Server Component serialization (for arguments) is more restrictive than Client Component serialization (for return values). This means you can return JSX elements but cannot accept them as arguments unless using pass-through patterns. 00156| 00157| ### Supported types 00158| 00159| **Arguments:** 00160| 00161| - Primitives: `string`, `number`, `boolean`, `null`, `undefined` 00162| - Plain objects: `{ key: value }` 00163| - Arrays: `[1, 2, 3]` 00164| - Dates, Maps, Sets, TypedArrays, ArrayBuffers 00165| - React elements (as pass-through only) 00166| 00167| **Return values:** 00168| 00169| - Same as arguments, plus JSX elements 00170| 00171| ### Unsupported types 00172| 00173| - Class instances 00174| - Functions (except as pass-through) 00175| - Symbols, WeakMaps, WeakSets 00176| - URL instances 00177| 00178| ```tsx filename="app/components/user-card.tsx" 00179| // Valid - primitives and plain objects 00180| async function UserCard({ 00181| id, 00182| config, 00183| }: { 00184| id: string 00185| config: { theme: string } 00186| }) { 00187| 'use cache' 00188| return
{id}
00189| } 00190| 00191| // Invalid - class instance 00192| async function UserProfile({ user }: { user: UserClass }) { 00193| 'use cache' 00194| // Error: Cannot serialize class instance 00195| return
{user.name}
00196| } 00197| ``` 00198| 00199| ### Pass-through (non-serializable arguments) 00200| 00201| You can accept non-serializable values **as long as you don't introspect them**. This enables composition patterns with `children` and Server Actions: 00202| 00203| ```tsx filename="app/components/cached-wrapper.tsx" 00204| async function CachedWrapper({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) { 00205| 'use cache' 00206| // Don't read or modify children - just pass it through 00207| return ( 00208|

{/* ... */}
00232| } 00233| ``` 00234| 00235| ## Constraints 00236| 00237| Cached functions execute in an isolated environment. The following constraints ensure cache behavior remains predictable and secure. 00238| 00239| ### Request-time APIs 00240| 00241| Cached functions and components **cannot** access runtime APIs like `cookies()`, `headers()`, or `searchParams`, and the restriction follows the call stack: a helper the cached function calls that reads one of these fails the same way, with the [`next-request-in-use-cache`](/docs/messages/next-request-in-use-cache) error. On a dynamically rendered route this surfaces when the route runs, so it can pass `next build` and fail under `next start`. Read these values outside the cached scope and pass them as arguments. 00242| 00243| ### Runtime caching considerations 00244| 00245| While `use cache` is designed primarily to include uncached data in the static shell, it can also cache data at runtime using in-memory LRU (Least Recently Used) storage. 00246| 00247| With the default in-memory handler, runtime cache behavior depends on your hosting environment: 00248| 00249| | Environment | Runtime Caching Behavior | 00250| | --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | 00251| | **Serverless** | Cache entries typically don't persist across requests (each request can be a different instance), or during revalidation. Build-time caching works normally. | 00252| | **Self-hosted** | Cache entries persist across requests. Control cache size with [`cacheMaxMemorySize`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheMaxMemorySize). | 00253| 00254| For example, in a serverless environment, a cached function shared by two pages executes on each static shell revalidation, whereas in self-hosted or environments with persistent memory, the cached output is reused if it's still fresh. 00255| 00256| If the default in-memory cache isn't enough, consider **[`use cache: remote`](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache-remote)** which allows platforms to provide a dedicated cache handler (like Redis or KV database). This helps reduce hits against data sources not scaled to your total traffic, though it comes with costs (storage, network latency, platform fees). 00257| 00258| > [!NOTE] 00259| > With the default in-memory handler, serverless instances are ephemeral, so entries may not be reused between requests, unlike with `use cache: remote`. Neither caching directive carries over to a new deploy, because the [cache key](#cache-keys) includes the build (or `deploymentId`) ID. 00260| > 00261| > For data that needs to persist across deploys, use [`unstable_cache`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/unstable_cache) for non-`fetch` functions or the [`fetch`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/fetch) cache. 00262| 00263| Very rarely, for compliance requirements or when you can't refactor your code to pass runtime data as arguments to a `use cache` scope, you might need [`use cache: private`](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache-private). 00264| 00265| ### Draft Mode 00266| 00267| When [Draft Mode](/docs/app/guides/draft-mode) is enabled, all cached functions and components re-execute on every request, and results are not saved to the cache. This ensures draft content is always fresh without requiring any changes to your caching code. 00268| 00269| You can read `isEnabled` from [`draftMode()`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/draft-mode) inside a `use cache` scope, however, other runtime APIs like `cookies()` and `headers()` are not allowed, even when Draft Mode is active. See [Passing runtime values to cached functions](/docs/app/getting-started/caching#passing-runtime-values-to-cached-functions) for the recommended pattern. 00270| 00271| ```tsx filename="app/components/content.tsx" 00272| import { draftMode } from 'next/headers' 00273| 00274| async function Content() { 00275| 'use cache' 00276| 00277| const { isEnabled } = await draftMode() 00278| const url = isEnabled 00279| ? 'https://draft.example.com/content' 00280| : 'https://production.example.com/content' 00281| 00282| const data = await fetch(url) 00283| return
{/* ... */}
00284| } 00285| ``` 00286| 00287| Calling `enable()` or `disable()` inside a caching directive scope will also throw an error. Draft Mode can only be toggled in [Route Handlers](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route) or [Server Actions](/docs/app/getting-started/mutating-data). 00288| 00289| ### React.cache isolation 00290| 00291| [`React.cache`](https://react.dev/reference/react/cache) operates in an isolated scope inside `use cache` boundaries. Values stored via `React.cache` outside a `use cache` function are not visible inside it. 00292| 00293| This means you cannot use `React.cache` to pass data into a `use cache` scope: 00294| 00295| ```tsx 00296| import { cache } from 'react' 00297| 00298| const store = cache(() => ({ current: null as string | null })) 00299| 00300| function Parent() { 00301| const shared = store() 00302| shared.current = 'value from parent' 00303| return 00304| } 00305| 00306| async function Child() { 00307| 'use cache' 00308| const shared = store() 00309| // shared.current is null, not 'value from parent' 00310| // use cache has its own isolated React.cache scope 00311| return
{shared.current}
00312| } 00313| ``` 00314| 00315| This isolation ensures cached functions have predictable, self-contained behavior. To pass data into a `use cache` scope, use function arguments instead. 00316| 00317| ## `use cache` at runtime 00318| 00319| On the **server**, cache entries are stored in-memory and respect the `revalidate` and `expire` times from your `cacheLife` configuration. You can customize the cache storage by configuring [`cacheHandlers`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheHandlers) in your `next.config.js` file. 00320| 00321| On the **client**, content from the server cache is stored in the browser's memory for the duration defined by the `stale` time. The client router enforces a **minimum 30-second stale time**, regardless of configuration. 00322| 00323| The `x-nextjs-stale-time` response header communicates cache lifetime from server to client, ensuring coordinated behavior. 00324| 00325| ## Revalidation 00326| 00327| Cached functions revalidate based on the `revalidate` and `expire` times in their `cacheLife` profile, or on-demand through tags. These two approaches are not mutually exclusive and are often paired: 00328| 00329| - **[Time-based](#time-based-revalidation)**: refresh automatically after a set duration with [`cacheLife`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheLife). 00330| - **[On-demand](#on-demand-revalidation)**: invalidate after a mutation with [`cacheTag`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheTag) and [`revalidateTag`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/revalidateTag) or [`updateTag`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/updateTag). 00331| 00332| For example, a blog post that changes only when its author edits it can use a long `cacheLife` like `max` with a `cacheTag`, then invalidate on demand when the post is saved. A list of recent posts that updates throughout the day can use a shorter profile like `hours` to refresh on its own, without manual invalidation. 00333| 00334| ### Time-based revalidation 00335| 00336| Set an explicit cache lifetime with [`cacheLife`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheLife) in every `use cache` scope. It makes the cache behavior clear at the call site, instead of depending on the `default` profile or surrounding caches. 00337| 00338| ```tsx filename="lib/data.ts" 00339| import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache' 00340| 00341| async function getData() { 00342| 'use cache' 00343| cacheLife('hours') // Use built-in 'hours' profile 00344| const res = await fetch('https://api.example.com/data') 00345| return res.json() 00346| } 00347| ``` 00348| 00349| If you omit `cacheLife`, the `default` profile applies and the lifetime is no longer explicit at the call site: 00350| 00351| - **stale**: 5 minutes (client-side) 00352| - **revalidate**: 15 minutes (server-side) 00353| - **expire**: never expires by time 00354| 00355| ```tsx filename="lib/data.ts" 00356| async function getData() { 00357| 'use cache' 00358| // Implicitly uses the 'default' profile 00359| const res = await fetch('https://api.example.com/data') 00360| return res.json() 00361| } 00362| ``` 00363| 00364| Nesting a short-lived use cache inside one without an explicit [cacheLife](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheLife) fails the build during prerendering. See [Nested short-lived caches](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheLife#nested-short-lived-caches) for the rule and fix. 00365| 00366| ### On-demand revalidation 00367| 00368| Use [`cacheTag`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheTag), [`updateTag`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/updateTag), or [`revalidateTag`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/revalidateTag) for on-demand cache invalidation: 00369| 00370| ```tsx filename="lib/data.ts" 00371| import { cacheTag } from 'next/cache' 00372| 00373| async function getProducts() { 00374| 'use cache' 00375| cacheTag('products') 00376| const res = await fetch('https://api.example.com/products') 00377| return res.json() 00378| } 00379| ``` 00380| 00381| ```tsx filename="app/actions.ts" 00382| 'use server' 00383| 00384| import { updateTag } from 'next/cache' 00385| 00386| export async function updateProduct() { 00387| await db.products.update(...) 00388| updateTag('products') // Invalidates all 'products' caches 00389| } 00390| ``` 00391| 00392| Both `cacheLife` and `cacheTag` integrate across client and server caching layers, meaning you configure your caching semantics in one place and they apply everywhere. 00393| 00394| ## Examples 00395| 00396| ### Caching function output with `use cache` 00397| 00398| You can add `use cache` to any asynchronous function, not only to components and routes. You might want to cache a network request, a database query, or a slow computation. 00399| 00400| ```tsx filename="app/actions.ts" highlight={2} switcher 00401| export async function getData() { 00402| 'use cache' 00403| 00404| const res = await fetch('https://api.example.com/data') 00405| const data = await res.json() 00406| return data 00407| } 00408| ``` 00409| 00410| ```jsx filename="app/actions.js" highlight={2} switcher 00411| export async function getData() { 00412| 'use cache' 00413| 00414| const res = await fetch('https://api.example.com/data') 00415| const data = await res.json() 00416| return data 00417| } 00418| ``` 00419| 00420| ### Caching a component's output with `use cache` 00421| 00422| You can use `use cache` at the component level to cache any fetches or computations performed within that component. The cache entry will be reused as long as the serialized props produce the same value in each instance. 00423| 00424| ```tsx filename="app/components/bookings.tsx" highlight={2} switcher 00425| export async function Bookings({ type = 'haircut' }: BookingsProps) { 00426| 'use cache' 00427| async function getBookingsData() { 00428| const response = await fetch( 00429| `https://api.example.com/bookings?type=${encodeURIComponent(type)}` 00430| ) 00431| const data = await response.json() 00432| return data 00433| } 00434| return //... 00435| } 00436| 00437| interface BookingsProps { 00438| type: string 00439| } 00440| ``` 00441| 00442| ```jsx filename="app/components/bookings.js" highlight={2} switcher 00443| export async function Bookings({ type = 'haircut' }) { 00444| 'use cache' 00445| async function getBookingsData() { 00446| const response = await fetch( 00447| `https://api.example.com/bookings?type=${encodeURIComponent(type)}` 00448| ) 00449| const data = await response.json() 00450| return data 00451| } 00452| return //... 00453| } 00454| ``` 00455| 00456| ### Interleaving 00457| 00458| In React, composition with `children` or slots is a well-known pattern for building flexible components. When using `use cache`, you can continue to compose your UI in this way. Anything included as `children`, or other compositional slots, in the returned JSX will be passed through the cached component without affecting its cache entry. 00459| 00460| As long as you don't directly reference any of the JSX slots inside the body of the cacheable function itself, their presence in the returned output won't affect the cache entry. 00461| 00462| ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" switcher 00463| export default async function Page() { 00464| const uncachedData = await getData() 00465| return ( 00466| // Pass compositional slots as props, e.g. header and children 00467| Home}> 00468| {/* DynamicComponent is provided as the children slot */} 00469| 00470| 00471| ) 00472| } 00473| 00474| async function CacheComponent({ 00475| header, // header: a compositional slot, injected as a prop 00476| children, // children: another slot for nested composition 00477| }: { 00478| header: ReactNode 00479| children: ReactNode 00480| }) { 00481| 'use cache' 00482| const res = await fetch('https://api.example.com/cached-data') 00483| const cachedData = await res.json() 00484| return ( 00485|

00490| ) 00491| } 00492| ``` 00493| 00494| ```jsx filename="app/page.js" switcher 00495| export default async function Page() { 00496| const uncachedData = await getData() 00497| return ( 00498| // Pass compositional slots as props, e.g. header and children 00499| Home}> 00500| {/* DynamicComponent is provided as the children slot */} 00501| 00502| 00503| ) 00504| } 00505| 00506| async function CacheComponent({ 00507| header, // header: a compositional slot, injected as a prop 00508| children, // children: another slot for nested composition 00509| }) { 00510| 'use cache' 00511| const res = await fetch('https://api.example.com/cached-data') 00512| const cachedData = await res.json() 00513| return ( 00514|

Every exported function it covers must be async. 00592| 00593| ```tsx filename="app/lib/reports.ts" 00594| 'use cache' 00595| 00596| export async function getMonthlyTotals(accountId: string) { 00597| return db.orders.aggregate({ where: { accountId }, _sum: { amount: true } }) 00598| } 00599| 00600| export async function getTopProducts() { 00601| return db.products.findMany({ orderBy: { sales: 'desc' }, take: 10 }) 00602| } 00603| ``` 00604| 00605| Framework function exports are covered like any other, so [`generateMetadata`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/generate-metadata) and [`generateStaticParams`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/generate-static-params) must be async in such a file. 00606| 00607| > **Good to know**: 00608| > 00609| > - When a cached directive (`use cache`, [`use cache: private`](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache-private), or [`use cache: remote`](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache-remote)) is at the top of a file, you can import its exported functions into a Client Component and call them directly; they run on the server and return the result, similar to a [Server Function](/docs/app/glossary#server-function). Prefer calling cached functions on the server and passing results down as props. 00610| 00611| ### Caching a route segment's output with `use cache` 00612| 00613| A `page` or `layout` file is a module too, so a file-level directive there follows the same rules. Each route segment is a separate entry point and is cached independently. To prerender a whole route, add `use cache` to the top of every segment file it renders: the `page`, the `layout`, and any [parallel route](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/parallel-routes) slots. 00614| 00615| ```tsx filename="app/layout.tsx" switcher 00616| 'use cache' 00617| 00618| export default async function Layout({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) { 00619| return
{children}

The `use cache` directive allows you to mark a route, React component, or a function as cacheable. It can be used at the top of a file to indicate that all exports in the file should be cached, or inline at the top of a function or component to cache the return value. Functions and components that use `use cache` must be async.
